chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Dharih, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When the Quraysh went out to Badr, and they took the sons of Abdul-Muttalib with them, Talib ibn Abi Talib went out. Their poetic chanters descended (began chanting) while they were chanting, and Talib ibn Abi Talib descended (began chanting) and said: 'O Lord, if they invade with Talib, in a group from these groups, in a group of the conquering, the fighter, make him the plundered, not the plunderer, and make him the conquered, not the conqueror.' So the Quraysh said, 'This one will conquer us,' so they sent him back. And in another report from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) is that he was a Muslim.

key_terms.بَدْرٌ: Badr, the location of the first major battle in Islam
key_terms.رُجَّازُهُمْ: Their poetic chanters / those reciting rajaz poetry
key_terms.طَالِبُ بْنُ أَبِي طَالِبٍ: Talib ibn Abi Talib, cousin of the Prophet Muhammad
key_terms.قُرَيْشٌ: Quraysh, the dominant tribe of Mecca

ai.seo_question: What did Talib ibn Abi Talib say during the Battle of Badr that caused the Quraysh to send him back?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Kafi* highlights Talib ibn Abi Talib’s unique spiritual stance during the Battle of Badr, where he recited a poetic invocation (*rujjaz*) asking God to make him the 'conquered' rather than the 'conqueror,' a paradox that led the Quraysh to dismiss him as a threat and send him back. The alternative report noting his prior conversion to Islam underscores the early, often concealed, presence of the Ahl al-Bayt within the Quraysh ranks, illustrating the theme of divine wisdom in preserving the Prophet’s lineage during critical historical moments. This event is often cited by Shia scholars to demonstrate Tal’s piety and his distinct role as a bridge between the Quraysh and the emerging Islamic community.
